newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UNHCR chief says Zaire rebels blocking refugee aid.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR chief says Zaire rebels blocking refugee aid.

text.p: U.N. High Commissioner For Refugees Sadako Ogata accused Tutsi-dominated rebels on Monday of blocking plans to repatriate up to 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees stuck in Zaire.
Ogata said each day's delay would cause more deaths among the refugees and appealed to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan to help get a troubled repatriation plan off the ground.
After talks with the visiting U.N. Secretary-General, Ogata said she asked for his strong support for the repatriation plan, delayed repeatedly by mounting rebel formalities in the chaotic region.
"There seems to be an attempt to block assistance coming in to the refugees. I feel there is a blockage. A day lost is hundreds of lives lost," Ogata told Reuters.
"They (the rebels) haven't been very helpful. It's been very frustrating, very difficult."

Ogata said the rebels on Monday forced another suspension of UNHCR's work at the camps south of the eastern city of Kisangani for security reasons after they began a military operation at the refugee camp of Kasese.
The operation raised the prospect of another refugee exodus, Ogata said.
The Rwandans are the rump of more than two million Hutus who fled in 1994 after the victory of Tutsi rebels in the civil war and the Hutu-led genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates.
Most went home late last year, but up to 300,000 fled deeper into Zaire where they have been on the run for five months.

UNHCR's plan to airlift a first group of some 80 refugee children was shelved on Friday after the rebels requisitioned the aviation fuel needed for the operation and demanded further medical checks on cholera cases reported among the Hutus.
The agency says cholera is not an obstacle to the airlift.
"The operation has been blocked so much -- for clearance, then local animosity, cholera...," Ogata said.
"Their (the rebels') basic position has been that they'd like all the refugees taken back. But this is a contradiction."
Privately, some aid officials said they feared the rebels could be trying to dress-up a shift in policy over repatriation.

They say this could be either because Rwanda is becoming overwhelmed after months of refugees returning and is putting pressure on the rebels to halt the repatriation, or it could indicate a split between rebel leaders and local authorities.
Ogata said she hoped to put pressure on the rebels and regional governments to try to take the refugees out.
In response to a question, she said Washington was also making contacts.

Diplomats and aid officials say rebel leader Laurent Kabila is refusing to talk to relief agency chiefs, but has spoken to U.S. president Bill Clinton's special envoy for Africa's troubled Great Lakes region, Richard Bogosian, at least once by telephone recently.
